opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a common conflation of transformers and sequence modeling, partly because of history: transformers came out of machine translation and took off with language models, so people think of them as sequence models. I'd argue that's not quite right.

At its core, a transformer is a model of **sets**. Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: if you shuffle the inputs, the outputs get shuffled the same way. The architecture itself has no notion of order. The only thing that makes it a sequence model is that we bolt on positional encodings, and for language, a causal mask. Those are design choices layered on top, not intrinsic properties.

So the way I'd put it is that transformers are general-purpose machines for processing sets of vectors, where every element can talk to every other element. Sequences are one structure you can impose on that set, but you can just as easily impose others. In vision you chop an image into patches and give them 2D positional information. In 3D you might have point clouds, Gaussians, or tokens attached to camera rays. In multimodal models you mix text tokens, image tokens, and audio tokens in one big set. The same machinery handles all of it, and that's a big part of why transformers have become the default everywhere.

Compare that to the architectures that came before. An RNN really is a sequence model: it processes one element at a time and carries state forward, so order is built into the computation. A ConvNet bakes in a grid structure with locality and translation equivariance. Those inductive biases helped when data and compute were scarce. But as we've scaled up, it turns out it's often better to have an architecture with weaker built-in assumptions and let the model learn the structure from data. You inject the structure you care about through the positional encoding and the masking.

There's also a hardware angle that I think is underappreciated. Transformers fit GPUs really well. The core operations are big matrix multiplies, and you process the whole set in parallel during training rather than stepping through time like an RNN. A lot of their success isn't just that attention is a clever idea. It's that it's a clever idea that maps onto the hardware we've been scaling.

That said, the sequence view still matters for generation. Autoregressive decoding is inherently sequential: you produce one token, append it, produce the next. That's where the costs show up, like the KV cache growing and attention being quadratic in context length. That's why there's so much interest in state-space models, linear attention, and hybrids that try to recover some RNN-like efficiency. So the picture is roughly this: transformers are fundamentally set processors, we often use them as sequence models, and a lot of current architecture research is about how much of the old sequential structure we want to bring back for efficiency without losing what made transformers work.

For the kind of work I care about, which is spatial intelligence and 3D worlds, that framing really matters. The world isn't a 1D sequence. If you think of transformers only as sequence models, you might try to flatten everything into a line of tokens. If you think of them as set models, the question becomes: what are the right elements, and what structure do I give them? That's a much richer design space.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that, at its core, a transformer is a model of sets and describes self-attention as permutation-equivariant.

r002.rationale: It attributes the sequence-model association to transformers' history in machine translation and language modeling. It mentions RNNs separately but does not say they caused that association.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that took me a while to really internalize is that the transformer isn't fundamentally a sequence model at all. It just happens to be the thing that killed the previous sequence models, so people conflate the two.

If you look at the architectures that came before, RNNs, LSTMs, even the convolutional sequence models, they all bake in a very strong prior about order. The computation literally flows left to right, or at least along a one-dimensional axis, and the inductive bias is that nearby things in the sequence should interact more than far-away things. That's a reasonable prior for language, and it's why those models worked as well as they did for a long time.

The transformer throws that away. If you strip out the positional encodings, attention is a set operation. It doesn't know what comes first or last, it just has a bunch of tokens and lets every token look at every other token and decide what to pull from. The "sequence-ness" is something you add back in as a side channel, through positional embeddings or RoPE or whatever flavor you like. So from my perspective, the transformer is really a general architecture for sets of tokens with learned pairwise interactions, and sequence modeling is one specific thing you can configure it to do.

That framing matters a lot to me because I come from the vision side, and it's exactly why the same architecture ports so cleanly to images, video, 3D, point clouds. Patches of an image are not a sequence in any meaningful sense, but they are a set of tokens, and if you tell the model where each one lives, attention handles the rest. The same thing is true for multimodal models where you're mixing text tokens and image tokens in one context. Nothing about that would make sense if the transformer were truly a sequence architecture.

Now, the one place where sequence really does come back is autoregressive decoding. The causal mask and the next-token objective are a genuinely sequential thing, and a huge amount of the practical success of LLMs comes from that training recipe rather than from the architecture per se. I'd actually argue the recipe is doing more of the work than people give it credit for. The transformer is a great substrate because it's parallel at training time and scales well on GPUs, but the thing that makes it feel like a sequence model is the way we train it, not what it is.

So the short version is: transformers are set models with a positional side channel, and "sequence modeling" is one very successful application of them that happens to be the one everybody encountered first.

r001.rationale: The response calls attention a set operation without positional encodings and describes transformers as “set models with a positional side channel.”

r002.rationale: It links the association to transformers replacing earlier sequence models, including RNNs, but does not say transformers’ historical roots lie in recurrent neural network architectures.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate the problem from the architecture. Sequence modeling is the problem: you have a sequence of things, and you want to understand the relationships between them or predict what comes next. A transformer is an architecture that you can use to solve that problem.

Before transformers, recurrent networks were a common approach. They process a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state forward. With a transformer, attention lets each position directly access other positions in the sequence, subject to whatever masking you impose. That gives you a different way to move information around, and it allows much more parallel computation during training.

But transformers aren’t inherently limited to sequences in the way that we sometimes assume from their association with language. You can turn an image into a collection of patch tokens, for example, and apply the same machinery. You need to represent the relevant structure—like position—but attention itself is a fairly general operation for letting elements interact. So sequence modeling is a major application of transformers, rather than their whole identity.

r001.rationale: The response describes attention as a general way for elements to interact and gives image patches as an example, but it does not state that transformers natively model sets.

r002.rationale: It says recurrent networks were common before transformers, but does not attribute transformers’ association with sequence modeling to historical roots in recurrent architectures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the problem from the architecture. Sequence modeling is the problem: you have an ordered set of things—words, audio samples, actions—and you want to model the relationships between them, often to predict what comes next. A transformer is one architecture for doing that.

Before transformers, recurrent networks were a common approach. They process a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state forward. Transformers instead use attention, so each position can directly access information from other positions. In a causal language model, that means attending to earlier tokens. That gives you a different way to handle dependencies, and it lets you parallelize computation across positions during training, although generation is still typically sequential.

But transformers are broader than sequence modeling. You can apply them to image patches or other collections of tokens. The architecture itself doesn’t inherently know the order; you need to provide positional information or impose structure through an attention mask. So sequence modeling is a particularly successful application of transformers, rather than a synonym for them.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers can operate on collections of tokens and that the architecture itself does not inherently know their order, which communicates set-like modeling by default.

r002.rationale: It mentions recurrent networks as a common pre-transformer approach, but does not attribute transformers’ association with sequence modeling to historical roots in recurrent architectures.
